{{nihongo|'''Achi Shrine'''|阿智神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Shinano Province]].

It is a {{ill|Shikinaisha|fr|Shikinaisha|zh|式內社|qid=Q134917286|lt=Shikinaisha}}, and under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|Q712534|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|lt=former shrine rank}} it was classified as a {{ill|Gō-sha|ja|郷社|qid=Q134917316}}. According to the “{{ill|Kujiki|Q2716751|qid=Q2716751}},” {{ill|Omoikane|Q586088|qid=Q586088|lt=Ame-no-Yagokoro-Omoikane-no-Mikoto}} descended from heaven and became the ancestor of the {{ill|Achi clan|Q109594403|qid=Q109594403|lt=Shinano no Achi Hafuribe}}, making this an ancient shrine with a venerable history.

=== History ===
According to shrine tradition, in the spring of the first month of the 5th year of {{ill|Emperor Kōgen|Q333572|qid=Q333572}}, {{ill|Omoikane|Q586088|qid=Q586088|lt=Ame-no-Yagokoro-Omoikane-no-Mikoto}} descended to Shinano Province accompanied by his divine children and became the ancestor of the {{ill|Achi clan|Q109594403|qid=Q109594403|lt=Achi no Hafuribe}}. The rituals were thereafter carried out by the Hara clan, his descendants.

This area lay along the route of the ancient {{ill|Tōsandō|Q1334011|qid=Q1334011}}. The place name Hirugami, the site of the shrine, is said to originate from a legend in which {{ill|Yamato Takeru|lt=Yamato Takeru|qid=Q461258}} was returning from his eastern campaign and attempted to cross {{ill|Misaka Pass|Q11588847|qid=Q11588847}}, but was blocked by the poisonous miasma of violent deities dwelling there. When he happened to spit out the garlic he was chewing, the evil gods immediately fell, allowing him to proceed. Because of this, the area was called Hirugami (“garlic-chewing”), which later became Hirugami (“day god”).

Another theory holds that Omoikane, who descended to this land, was the foremost god of wisdom in Takamagahara, devising plans for all affairs and bringing them to fruition. In particular, when {{ill|Amaterasu|Q455602|qid=Q455602}}, angered by the outrageous behavior of her brother {{ill|Susanoo-no-Mikoto|lt=Susanoo-no-Mikoto|qid=Q272993}}, hid herself in the {{ill|Amano-Iwato|Q3231835|qid=Q3231835|lt=Heavenly Rock Cave}}, it was through Omoikane’s direction that the sun goddess Amaterasu was safely brought back outside. Because Omoikane rendered such great service—returning the world from darkness to daylight—the place where he settled is said to be called Hirugami (“day god”).

The Okumiya lies about 2 kilometers upstream from the Maemiya along the {{ill|Achi River|Q110454496|qid=Q110454496}}, at the triangular, peninsula-like point where the Motodani River and the Kurokawa River merge to form the Achi River, a place known as Kawaigaryō. On the hilltop stands a moss-covered giant rock that is venerated. {{ill|Iwao Ōba|Q11433904|qid=Q11433904}}, a professor at {{ill|Kokugakuin University|Q495330|qid=Q495330}}, demonstrated that this rock is an {{ill|Iwakura rock|Q11587880|qid=Q11587880}}, that is, a relic of ancient {{ill|Shinto ritual|Q109937652|qid=Q109937652|lt=ritual practices}}<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|Japanese|title=Achi Village History, Volume 1|date=1984-03-20|year=1984|publisher=Achi Village History Publication Committee}}</ref>. Although it is a naturally formed giant stone close to a diamond shape, its protrusions are said to align with the four cardinal directions. It is also said that at the time of the winter solstice, the sun rises along its eastern extension.

It is said that during the Tenryaku era under the reign of Emperor Murakami, the Tokutake clan enshrined as branch deities at the Nakasha (enshrined deity: Ame-no-Yagokoro-Omoikane-no-Mikoto) and Hōkōsha (enshrined deity: Ame-no-Uwaharu-no-Mikoto) of {{ill|Togakushi Shrine|Q218828|qid=Q218828}}, formerly a national shrine located in Togakushi Village, Kamiminochi District<ref>{{Cite book|Japanese|author=|title=Shimoina History, Vol. 4, Shimoina History Compilation Committee, Representative Ichimura Kaneto|date=|year=1961|publisher=Shinano Education Association Publishing Department}}</ref>. For a time, it was also called {{ill|Sannō Gongen|Q11470054|qid=Q11470054|lt=Sannō Gongen Shrine}}, as confirmed by {{ill|shuinjō|Q11093673|qid=Q11093673}} (vermillion seal documents).

In addition, {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Amekaharu-no-Mikoto}}, the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Kuni no miyatsuko|Q2483673|qid=Q2483673}} and an enshrined deity of {{ill|Chichibu Shrine|Q2963366|qid=Q2963366}} in {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|Q128186|qid=Q128186}}, which was worshipped by the {{ill|Chichibu Province|Q5096034|qid=Q5096034}}, is said to be the younger brother of Ame-no-Uwaharu-no-Mikoto<ref name=":0" />.

According to the “{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Saibe-shi Kaden}},” {{ill|Ame-no-Tajikarao|Q849412|qid=Q849412}} is said to be a distant ancestor of the Achi Hafuri.
